Highlight

FULL VIEW
OUTLINE VIEW
Pretest
Discover What You Know
Learning Objectives
Recognize risk factors that lead to the formation of heterotopic ossification after total hip
arthroplasty.
Understand prevention strategies for patients at high risk for heterotopic ossification.
Comprehend the timing and treatment options for the management of postoperative
heterotopic ossification.
Introduction
Definition
Heterotopic ossification involves extra-skeletal normal lamellar bone formation in soft tissues.




NOTES

Causes
Trauma
Connective-tissue diseases
Ankylosing spondylitis and diffuse idiopathic skeletal hyperostosis

Causes
Numerous conditions may result in this phenomenon, including traumatic neurogenic
injury, blast and burn injuries, dislocations, and musculoskeletal trauma.1 Various
connective-tissue diseases, such as fibrodysplasia progressive ossificans, also are
associated with heterotopic ossification formation.1 Ankylosing spondylitis and diffuse
idiopathic skeletal hyperostosis also may lead to heterotopic ossification.2 Heterotopic
ossification is a frequent complication (8% to 90%) after hip arthroplasty.3,4
Incidence

Incidence
An incidence of heterotopic ossification as high as 60% recently was reported among 651
patients who underwent hip arthroplasty.5 As increasing numbers of patients undergo
this type of surgical procedure, the incidence of heterotopic ossification also is likely to
increase. Given the recent increase in the use of NSAIDs (in addition to aspirin) as part of
multimodal analgesia for thromboembolic prophylaxis in acetabular fracture surgery,
the rate of heterotopic ossification has been reported to have declined substantially
compared with a control group (30% versus 45.8%; P = 0.011).6
Patient Presentation
Persistent pain
Prolonged fever
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:47 PM

Restricted range of motion
Swelling and erythema (may mimic infection)

Patient Presentation
From a clinical standpoint, patients with heterotopic ossification may present with
persistent pain, prolonged fever, overlying skin erythema, restricted range of motion
(ROM), and swelling. Some resolution of symptoms likely happens after 1 year.3 These
symptoms may mimic postoperative infection; therefore, a clear distinction must be
made between the two complications. From a radiographic standpoint, several
classification systems have been proposed for heterotopic ossification; however, the
Brooker classification, originally proposed in 1975, currently is the most commonly
accepted and used classification system for heterotopic ossification to.7-10 (Resource 1).
Heterotopic ossification usually occurs between 6 and 12 weeks after hip surgery and
matures by 1 year postoperatively.11
Rationale

Rationale
Despite such a high rate of occurrence after hip arthroplasty, not a single orthopaedic
association has established standard preventive guidelines and treatment principles for
heterotopic ossification.12 This complication is concerning because it greatly limits hip
ROM and suggests a likelihood of eventual revision hip arthroplasty. Therefore, this
lesson attempts to describe the classification of, risk factors for, preventive measures
for, and diagnostic and treatment guidelines for heterotopic ossification.
Classification Systems
Brooker classification
Modification of the Brooker classification

Della Valle classification system
Brooker Classification

Brooker Classification
Numerous classification systems have been proposed to grade heterotopic ossification
after total hip arthroplasty (THA). The Brooker classification (1973) was the first proposed
classification.7 Based on AP pelvic radiographs alone, the classification system
categorizes heterotopic ossification into four classes: class 1, bone islands within the soft
tissues about the hip; class 2, bone spurs originating from the pelvis or the proximal end
of the femur, leaving at least 1 cm between the opposing bone surfaces; class 3, bone
spurs originating from the pelvis or the proximal end of the femur, reducing the space
between the opposing bone surfaces to less than 1 cm; and class 4, apparent bone
ankylosis of the hip (Figure 1).

arthroplasty: Risk factors, prevention, and treatment. J Am Acad Orthop Surg
2002;10[6]:409-416.)
Modification of the Brooker Classification

Modification of the Brooker Classification
Because of high intraobserver and interobserver disagreement on the Brooker
classification, subsequent studies suggested modifications.13 Wright et al9 asserted that
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:47 PM
AAOS | Postoperative Heterotopic Ossification
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001027
5/30

bone formation limited to zones near osteotomy, bone graft, and fracture or proximal to
the superolateral acetabular lip/distal to the resected femoral neck should not be
considered heterotopic ossification. The authors also suggested that the ectopic bone
between the lesser trochanter and the ischium should fall into class 2 heterotopic
ossification, regardless of the space between the opposing bone surfaces.9 After
applying these principles to the heterotopic ossification classification system, the
authors demonstrated an improvement in interobserver reliability (from 0.57 to 0.68)
and overall agreement (from 68% to 77%) compared with the Brooker classification
system.
Della Valle Classification System

Della Valle Classification System
Another recent classification system was proposed by Della Valle et al.8 This
classification system places more emphasis on the clinical importance of heterotopic
ossification rather than radiographic features alone and disagrees with the
determination of ankylosis on AP radiographs in the Brooker classification system. The
authors reported that hips without heterotopic ossification on AP radiographic
evaluation and Brooker class I were categorized in the same class. In addition, Brooker
classes 3 and 4 were grouped together, and bone island size and spur separation
distance were not defined. The Della Valle classification system divided heterotopic
ossification into three grades: grade A, heterotopic ossification absent or greater than or
equal to one island of bone and less than 1 cm in length present; grade B, more than
one island of bone present, at least 1 cm in length, and the presence of bone spurs from
the pelvis or femur, leaving at least 1 cm between the opposing bone surfaces; and
grade C, presence of bone spurs from the pelvis or femur leaving less than 1 cm
between the opposing bone surfaces and apparent bone ankylosis.8
Brooker Versus Della Valle Classification Systems


Brooker Versus Della Valle Classification Systems
Recently, Vasileiadis et al14 investigated 236 patients with heterotopic ossification to
compare the Brooker classification system and the Della Valle classification system. The
Brooker system was associated with moderate to high intraobserver reliability (ranging
from 0.43 to 0.71);7 however, the Della Valle classification system was associated with
high intraobserver reliability (ranging from 0.65 to 0.77).8 Interobserver agreement was
moderate for both classification systems (0.40 to 0.60). The authors concluded that both
classification systems lacked sufficient precision and were associated with variable
subject interpretation.14
Risk Factors

Risk Factors
Identification of patients at risk for heterotopic ossification is key in the application of
preventive strategies. Numerous patient-related or surgery-related risk factors for
heterotopic ossification have been reported, including age, sex, type of osteoarthritis,
history of heterotopic ossification, type of anesthesia, and intraoperative blood
transfusion15-36 (Table 1).

Patient-Related Factors

Women older than 65 years have a substantially increased risk of postoperative
heterotopic ossification after THA.15 However, this finding is not true for men older than
65 years. Men in general have a substantially higher risk for this heterotopic ossification
after THA than women.11,15-20 Similar results recently were reported by Rüdiger et al,21
who found that older age in women (P < 0.005) and men (P < 0.05) was a considerable
risk factor for heterotopic ossification (Resource 2). DeLee et al11 followed up patients
who underwent Charnley low-friction arthroplasty and reported a threefold higher
occurrence of heterotopic ossification in males than females. The authors also
demonstrated that ipsilateral or contralateral heterotopic ossification was one of the
most important predictors of postoperative heterotopic ossification after THA because
this complication occurred in all hips in the study, with no exceptions. Similar results
were reported by Ritter and Vaughan17 and Nollen and van Douveren,18 who found that,
, postoperative heterotopic ossification occurred in 100% and 82% of patients with prior
heterotopic ossification, respectively.
Recently, Davis et al22 assessed the effect of ethnicity on the formation of heterotopic
ossification after THA by retrospectively reviewing 1,449 consecutive primary THA
procedures. African American patients had 2.6 and 1.9 higher risk of severe heterotopic
ossification formation and any heterotopic ossification grade, respectively, compared
with Caucasian patients. In multiple studies, the hypertrophic type of osteoarthritis also
has been shown to be an important risk factor in the formation of heterotopic
ossification.18,22-25 Patients with ankylosing spondylitis and diffuse idiopathic skeletal
hyperostosis also have an increased risk for heterotopic ossification.19,26
Surgery-Related Factors
Surgical time
Blood transfusion
Type of anesthesia during THA
Type of surgical approach
Type of implant
American Society of Anesthesiologists (ASA) grade
Type of incision

Type of fixation
Intra-articular drainage

Surgery-Related Factors
A surgical time exceeding 100 minutes is associated with a higher risk of heterotopic
ossification. Blood transfusion or type of anesthesia do not have any relationship with
heterotopic ossification.16,20 Complicated surgical procedures with increased surgical
time and damage to the soft tissues are considered to increase the risk of postoperative
heterotopic ossification.15,16,20 Conflicting results have been reported in other studies,
reporting a considerable association of blood transfusion and general plus spinal or
epidural anesthesia with the formation of heterotopic ossification after THA.15,16
Similarly, the evidence is contradictory with regard to the surgical approach and its effect
on the incidence of heterotopic ossification. Although many studies have demonstrated
a higher occurrence of heterotopic ossification with the anterior approach and a lower
occurrence with the posterior approach, several other studies have not reported a
statistically significant difference.11,16,19,25,27-29 Of the lateral approaches, the Liverpool
approach, in which a slice of bone is taken with the gluteal flap, is associated with a
higher rate of postoperative heterotopic ossification (65%) than the trans-trochanteric
(36%) and the Hardinge (24%) approaches, in which gluteus medius muscle is reflected in
continuity with the vastus lateralis muscle.30
Multiple recent studies have assessed surgical approaches as risk factors for heterotopic
ossification.31-33 Newman et al31 demonstrated lower rates of severe heterotopic
ossification (Brooker classes 3 and 4) with the direct anterior approach (DAA, 3% in grade
3; zero in grade 4) compared with the posterior approach (4.2% in grade 3; 3.3% in grade
4; P = 0.04) for THA. Similarly, Alijanipour et al32 compared the direct lateral approach
with the DAA and reported a lower overall incidence (19.4%) of heterotopic ossification
with the DAA than with the direct lateral approach (36.1%; P < 0.001). Hürlimann et al33
assessed 134 consecutive THA procedures and compared standard surgery with
minimally invasive surgery. The standard modified anterolateral approach correlated
with the highest rate of heterotopic ossification (45.2%), which was considerably

different from the minimally invasive DAA (23.1%; P = 0.020) and the standard
transgluteal Bauer approach (14.3%; P = 0.038).
The type of implant used also affects the occurrence of heterotopic ossification. Biz et al5
performed a multivariate analysis of 651 patients who underwent hip arthroplasty via
one of three types of implants: ceramic-ceramic, a polycarbonate urethane–ceramic, or
an endoprosthesis. Patients treated via the polycarbonate urethane–ceramic and
ceramic-ceramic implants had a 2 and 1.9 times higher risk, respectively, for
postoperative heterotopic ossification compared with patients treated with an
endoprosthesis. In a recent study based on a multivariate risk model, only an ASA grade
higher than 3 (P = 0.00011) and the type of incision (longitudinal versus bikini incision; P
= 0.008) substantially increased the risk of heterotopic ossification.21 Other variables,
such as surgeon experience, numbness, scar appearance, paresthesia, pruritus, or
postoperative pain did not have an association with postoperative heterotopic
ossification.21 The effect of fixation type on heterotopic ossification also has been
investigated in numerous studies.18,25,27,34,35 Although an increased risk of heterotopic
ossification in has been reported with noncemented fixation in some studies,
noncemented fixation currently is acknowledged as not being a risk factor for
heterotopic ossification.18,25,27,34,35
In addition to the already mentioned risk factors, Benedetto et al36 investigated 425 THA
procedures to determine the role of intraoperative drainage with regard to heterotopic
ossification after THA. The authors found that intra-articular drainage was substantially
associated with a high incidence of heterotopic ossification compared with no drainage
(24.6% versus 15.3%; P = 0.02). In addition to patient and surgical risk factors,
postoperative risk factors, including prolonged fever, hematoma, wound drainage, and
superficial wound drainage, also may increase the risk of heterotopic ossification.16,19
Clinical Importance
Mild heterotopic ossification (Brooker class 1 and class 2) has minimal effect on postoperative
pain or ROM.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:47 PM
AAOS | Postoperative Heterotopic Ossification
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001027
11/30

Only Brooker class 4 heterotopic ossification has been shown to affect clinical outcomes after
THA.
Severe heterotopic ossification results in substantial ROM restriction but does not result in
increased postoperative pain.

Clinical Importance
A risk of heterotopic ossification formation exists after THA; however, the effect of
heterotopic ossification on the postoperative clinical outcomes of patients is most
important. Overall, mild heterotopic ossification (Brooker classes 1 and 2) has a minimal
effect on postoperative pain or ROM. In one of the first follow-up studies, Charnley37
reported that prominent heterotopic ossification occurred in 5% of approximately 400
hips and deemed heterotopic ossification to be a matter of academic interest that had
no effect on clinical outcomes. Similar results were reported by Brooker et al,7 who
found that all Brooker heterotopic ossification classes, except class 4, did not affect
postoperative clinical outcomes after THA. Regardless, Kromann-Andersen et al38
reported that even low grades of heterotopic ossification resulted in reduced walking
ability and ROM of the hip at 2-year follow-up; however, the authors did not report any
association between pain and heterotopic ossification severity. The literature on the
worst cases of heterotopic ossification (Brooker classes 3 and 4) shows that severe
heterotopic ossification results in substantial restriction in ROM but does not result in
increased postoperative pain.7,27,37,39,40
Prevention

Prevention
The ideal solution is to prevent heterotopic ossification. Identification of patients at risk
for heterotopic ossification is imperative. Several prophylactic therapies have been
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:47 PM
AAOS | Postoperative Heterotopic Ossification
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001027
12/30

proposed for heterotopic ossification. Broadly, these therapies can be categorized as
drug therapy or radiation therapy.
Drug Therapy
NSAIDs
Cyclooxygenase-2 (COX-2) inhibitors
Aspirin
Diphosphonates

Drug Therapy
Conventional NSAIDs have been proven to be effective agents for heterotopic
ossification prophylaxis in multiple studies, systematic reviews, and meta-analyses.41-49
This group of drugs inhibits the production of proinflammatory prostaglandins, reducing
inflammation favorable for the development of heterotopic ossification. Fransen and
Neal42 performed a Cochrane review of as many as 17 level I studies on this subject and
found a 59% reduction in heterotopic ossification in patients being treated with NSAIDs
versus a placebo without greatly increasing the incidence of gastrointestinal adverse
effects.42 Another systematic review of 13 randomized controlled trials (RCTs)
demonstrated as much as a 57% reduction in overall heterotopic ossification risk
postoperatively with this drug therapy.41 Because of their gastrointestinal tolerance and
effectiveness in the prevention of heterotopic ossification, COX-2 inhibitors are a good
alternative. In a RCT, Saudan et al48 reported lower heterotopic ossification rates with
celecoxib versus ibuprofen, with no analysis of gastrointestinal adverse effects. However,
Vasileiadis et al49 reported no difference in heterotopic ossification rates between COX-2
inhibitors and standard NSAIDs; however, the authors reported fewer gastrointestinal
adverse effects with the use of COX-2 inhibitors.
Evidence from the most recent meta-analysis by Joice et al50 on the prophylactic use of
NSAIDs showed that nonselective and selective NSAIDs are equally effective choices for
prophylaxis (Resource 3). Another recent meta-analysis demonstrated that naproxen

9/3/26, 5:47 PM
AAOS | Postoperative Heterotopic Ossification
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001027
13/30

results in a substantial reduction in heterotopic ossification incidence at 1.5-month, 3-
month, 6-month, and 12-month follow-up, with no considerable increase in the
complication rate.51
Because aspirin is routinely prescribed for deep vein thrombosis (DVT) prophylaxis after
THA, its possible additional role as a prophylactic medication for heterotopic ossification
has been investigated. Regardless, evidence on the effectiveness of aspirin in preventing
heterotopic ossification is inconsistent. Based on a double-blind RCT performed by Neal
et al,44 a 162-mg/day aspirin intake for 35 days did not have any effect on the incidence
of heterotopic ossification compared with a placebo. In contrast to these results, studies
conducted by Nunley et al46 and Bek et al45 on bilateral one-stage THA and surface
replacement arthroplasty found a considerable reduction in the formation of
heterotopic ossification with 325 mg of aspirin administered twice per day compared
with coumadin used for DVT prophylaxis. These findings raised questions about the
dose-related efficacy of aspirin. In 2020, Vaz et al52 compared patients who underwent
THA and received DVT prophylaxis via aspirin against patients who underwent THA and
received non-aspirin chemoprophylaxis (Resource 4). Heterotopic ossification occurred
at a considerably higher rate in patients being treated with the non-aspirin regimen
(30.9%) compared with those being treated via aspirin prophylaxis (13.1%; P < 0.01).
Given the evidence supporting the use of COX-2 inhibitors for heterotopic ossification
prophylaxis, attention also must be paid to their cardiac adverse effects. Similarly,
because NSAIDs are known to inhibit bone formation, their possible effects on bone
ingrowth into noncemented THA components must be considered.44,53 The best
approach is to first identify at-risk patients who can be treated via heterotopic
ossification prophylaxis with NSAIDs.
Another set of drugs, diphosphonates, failed to prevent heterotopic ossification over the
long term despite promising short-term results. This outcome is related to their basic
mechanism, which does not prevent the deposition of osteoid but only mineralization.
Therefore, if these drugs are discontinued, deposited osteoid mineralizes and presents
as heterotopic ossification on imaging studies.54
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:47 PM

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001027
14/30

Radiation Therapy
Radiation therapy affects the responsiveness of the bone morphogenetic protein 2–receptor
complex to bone morphogenetic protein 2–induced osteoblast differentiation.
Findings on the association between radiation dosing and the occurrence of heterotopic
ossification are conflicting.
Although timely radiation therapy is recommended after THA, late low-dose radiation therapy
may prevent heterotopic ossification.
Combined radiation therapy and NSAIDs decreases the prevalence of heterotopic ossification
better than NSAIDs or radiation therapy alone.
No differences have been reported in the rate of heterotopic ossification with regard to
preoperative or postoperative radiation therapy.
The recommendations of the authors of this lesson are as follows: single dose of radiation
therapy (more than 700 rad) within 24 hours of the index procedure in combination with
NSAIDs for 2 weeks if tolerated.

Radiation Therapy
Because of its better adverse-effect profile, radiation therapy has been studied as an
alternative to NSAIDs. Various mechanisms have been proposed for the role of radiation
therapy in the management of heterotopic ossification. The currently accepted concept
is that radiation therapy affects the responsiveness of the bone morphogenetic protein
2–receptor complex to bone morphogenetic protein 2–induced osteoblast
differentiation.55
In one of the first studies performed after the inhibitory effect of radiation therapy on
vertebral growth in patients with abdominal cancer was observed, Coventry and
Scanlon56 developed a radiation therapy prophylactic protocol that involved 20 gray (Gy)
of radiation in 10 fractions over a span of 12 days, beginning from 2 to 10 days after
THA. At that time, this dose was not associated with any secondary malignancy. None of
the 11 of 3,204 hips managed via radiation therapy had recurrence of severe heterotopic
ossification. This finding paved the way for several studies evaluating the effect of timing,
dosing, and fractionation of radiation therapy used for heterotopic ossification
prophylaxis.4,57-63 With respect to dosing, Pellegrini et al62 found no difference between

9/3/26, 5:47 PM

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001027
15/30

8 Gy in a single fraction and a dosage of 10 Gy in five fractions; heterotopic ossification
occurred in 21% of patients in both groups. Similarly, Padgett et al64 found no difference
between single dosages of 5 Gy and 10 Gy. Contradictory findings have been reported.
Chao et al60 analyzed multiple radiation therapy protocols used at their institution: 20 Gy
in ten fractions and five fractions; 8 Gy in one fraction; 7 Gy in one fraction; and 6 Gy in
one fraction, three fractions, and two fractions. The authors found that 7 Gy in one
fraction was associated with a considerably lower rate of heterotopic ossification
formation (13.8%) compared with 6 Gy in two fractions (60%). Healy et al61 also found a
one-time dose of 7 Gy to be more effective than a single fraction of 5.5 Gy in a high-risk
patient population.
Radiation doses for the prophylaxis of heterotopic ossification have always been a topic
of discussion. In a recent RCT, Liu et al65 demonstrated that 700 Centigray was
considerably superior to 400 Centigray in preventing heterotopic ossification formation
after THA in high-risk patients. Using a myriad of radiation therapy strategies, Hu et al66
performed a systematic review and meta-analysis of RCTs to compare heterotopic
ossification progression with variable doses, timing, and frequency and explore an
optimal radiation therapy option. The authors concluded that radiation therapy with a
medium dose (20 Gy to 24 Gy) after THA is effective for heterotopic ossification
prophylaxis and found that multiple fractions are more effective than a single fraction of
radiation. The timely use of radiation therapy has been recommended for the
prevention of heterotopic ossification; however, Morcos et al67 reported that even late,
low-dose radiotherapy administered 6 to 12 weeks postoperatively in patients in whom
heterotopic ossification had already formed prevented the progression of heterotopic
ossification.
In a study comparing aspirin, indomethacin, and fractional or single-dose irradiation,
Knelles et al4 demonstrated that, compared with a control group, postoperative
radiation therapy (3 Gy in four fractions or 7 Gy in one fraction) and indomethacin (50
mg twice per day for 7 or 14 days) resulted in a substantial reduction in heterotopic
ossification formation. Heterotopic ossification occurred at a higher rate in the patients
being treated with aspirin and patients who received 5 Gy in one fraction than in those
being treated with indomethacin and with other radiation therapy dosages in the study.

The authors recommended the prophylactic use of indomethacin for all patients and
radiation therapy in high-risk patients or if NSAIDs were contraindicated.4
On analyzing a combined therapy of NSAIDs and radiation therapy for the prevention of
heterotopic ossification at a mean follow-up of 21 months, Wu et al68 reported that
combined therapy lowered the prevalence of heterotopic ossification better than NSAIDs
or radiation therapy alone; however, the difference did not reach statistical significance.
The authors still recommended NSAIDs as the first choice to prevent heterotopic
ossification after THA.
Varying protocols have been proposed for radiation therapy to prevent heterotopic
ossification. Koelbl et al57 compared preoperative radiation therapy with postoperative
radiation therapy and found that preoperative radiation therapy administered on the
evening before the scheduled surgery in high-risk patients was associated with an 18.1%
rate of overall heterotopic ossification and a 1.9% rate of severe heterotopic ossification,
which were comparable to the heterotopic ossification incidence observed with single-
fraction postoperative radiation therapy. Similarly, Pellegrini et al63 did not find any
considerable difference in heterotopic ossification rates (24% versus 27%) between
preoperative (less than 4 hours before THA) and postoperative (within 72 hours after
THA) 8 Gy radiation therapy in a one-fraction dose. Radiation therapy administered
preoperatively or postoperatively and in a single or multiple fractions was an effective
prophylaxis for heterotopic ossification, with no considerable carcinogenic potential at a
follow-up of 10 years after THA in a study by Pakos et al.69
The authors of this lesson recommend a single dose of radiation therapy (more than 700
rads) within 24 hours of the index procedure in combination with NSAIDs for 2 weeks if
the patient can tolerate them70 (Resource 5). The authors of this lesson recommend 81
mg of acetylsalicylic acid by mouth twice a day for DVT prophylaxis, which may have an
adjuvant effect in preventing heterotopic ossification formation.
Diagnosis and Management
Diagnosis
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:47 PM
AAOS | Postoperative Heterotopic Ossification
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001027
17/30

Serum Test
Erythrocyte sedimentation rate
C-reactive protein level

Serum Test
Prophylactic measures for heterotopic ossification are effective only before the
development of a nidus. Researchers are looking for a diagnostic test that can identify
the initiation of heterotopic ossification formation early in the disease process, at which
time prophylactic management may have an effect on the incidence of heterotopic
ossification. Inflammatory markers, such as the erythrocyte sedimentation rate and C-
reactive protein level, have been considered for that purpose.71 Evidence exists that
heterotopic ossification occurs at a substantially higher rate in patients who undergo
THA and have a high postoperative erythrocyte sedimentation rate ; however, this
occurred at minimum follow-up of 6 weeks, which is too late for any prophylactic
treatment to be effective.71 In another study, C-reactive protein levels were substantially
higher on the fifth postoperative day in patients with Brooker class II to IV heterotopic
ossification compared with patients with Brooker class I heterotopic ossification.72
Because of this late elevation, elevated values immediately postoperatively regardless of
other factors, and the possible effect of coprescribed NSAIDs on inflammation, these
inflammatory markers have limited value in the diagnosis of heterotopic ossification.
Imaging Studies
Plain radiography (preferred)
CT/MRI (preoperative planning)
Ultrasonography

Imaging Studies
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:47 PM

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001027
18/30

Currently, plain radiographs are the preferred diagnostic imaging study for heterotopic
ossification, which is observed as bone islands approximately 6 to 12 weeks after THA
and matures fully by 1 year postoperatively.7,8,11,17,18,23,54,59,60 A three-phase bone
scan can be used to diagnose heterotopic ossification much earlier, approximately 4 to 6
weeks postoperatively, before heterotopic ossification is visible on plain radiographs;73
however, a negative three-phase bone scan represents a fully matured heterotopic
ossification and is more commonly used to determine the timing of resection. Other
imaging studies, such as CT and MRI, may be helpful in providing a detailed anatomic
assessment of heterotopic ossification and in preoperative planning if surgical excision is
indicated.74,75 Similar to other imaging studies, ultrasonography can detect heterotopic
ossification before it is observed on radiographs; however, such detection remains
outside the time frame necessary to administer effective heterotopic ossification
prophylaxis.76
Indications
Pain at rest or during movement
Reduced ROM

Indications
Currently, the indications and treatment algorithm for heterotopic ossification are
unclear. Recently, a survey was conducted among orthopaedic and trauma departments
in Germany on therapeutic strategies to manage heterotopic ossification. The important
and very important indications for heterotopic ossification excision in this survey
included pain at rest, pain during joint movement, and reduced ROM77 (Resource 6).
Management
Excision in combination with postoperative prophylaxis via NSAIDs or radiation therapy is the
most common management strategy.

Surgical excision should be performed only after the maturation of heterotopic ossification,

To reduce blood loss, circumferential dissection and/or bipolar cautery is recommended.
In patients with severe blood loss, autologous blood transfusions with cell saver systems

Management
The management of heterotopic ossification involves excision in combination with
postoperative prophylaxis via NSAIDs or radiation therapy given the high recurrence rate
(Figure 2). Surgical excision alone has been shown to result in a high recurrence rate.
Therefore, postoperative prophylaxis is recommended.78 Surgical excision should be
performed only after the maturation of heterotopic ossification, which can be confirmed
on a bone scan. Otherwise, heterotopic ossification is more likely to recur and may result
in blood loss or neurovascular injury.79 In a study of 12 patients with heterotopic
ossification who underwent excision followed by prophylactic radiation therapy (variable
fractions and doses), only one patient who did not receive radiation therapy until 5 days
after THA had a recurrence of Brooker class II heterotopic ossification. The remaining 11
patients did not experience new heterotopic ossification formation.80

In a retrospective investigation, Cobb et al81 reviewed 52 patients with symptomatic
heterotopic ossification after THA who underwent surgical excision and postoperative
prophylaxis for clinical, functional, or radiographic indications. Of the 52 patients, 32
were treated for restricted ROM only, 14 were treated for restricted ROM and pain, 2
were treated for instability, and 5 were treated for pain only. Without exception,
treatment performed for all indications resulted in substantial improvement in ROM,
patient satisfaction, and reduction in radiographic heterotopic ossification. Because a
reduction in pain occurred in only one of five patients who underwent excision for this
reason, Cobb et al81 discouraged the excision of heterotopic ossification in patients with
pain alone.
In general, perioperative irradiation and oral NSAIDs prophylaxis in combination with
surgical management is the most common and accepted treatment option. An evidence-
based recommendation for the most effective prophylaxis is lacking. From a surgeon’s
perspective, depending on the location of heterotopic ossification, complete excision via
a single surgical approach is difficult. All steps, from preoperative planning with
orthogonal radiographs or CT scans to intraoperative distinction between normal and
heterotopic bone, should be considered. To reduce blood loss, circumferential dissection
completely around the margin of the heterotopic bone is preferred over piecemeal
excision. To reduce blood loss during such procedures, a method such as bipolar cautery
is recommended; in patients with severe blood loss, autologous blood transfusions with
cell saver systems should be administered.

Treatment Options Under Development
New experimental treatment options for heterotopic ossification are available that may
be valuable in the future. Diphosphonates are being considered, but their long-term
effect on heterotopic ossification remains elusive.82 Basic science research has found
that selective retinoic acid receptor gamma agonists suppress bone morphogenetic
protein signaling and chondrogenesis in a murine model.83 Substance P, mast cell
blockers, and cromolyn inhibitors also have been shown to result in a considerable
reduction in heterotopic ossification rates in animals.84 Regardless, these proposed
methods are in experimental stages.
Conclusion
The mechanism of heterotopic ossification development remains unknown.
No standard guidelines exist for the detection and management of heterotopic ossification.
Risk factors for heterotopic ossification must be recognized to initiate prophylaxis.
Surgeons should wait for at least 12 months before surgical excision of heterotopic ossification
unless heterotopic ossification is very severe.
Surgeons should recognize the risks of excessive bleeding and neurovascular injury during
heterotopic ossification excision

Conclusion
Heterotopic ossification is a common complication after THA. Many risk factors and
preventive strategies via NSAIDs and radiotherapy have been proposed; however, the
mechanism of heterotopic ossification development remains unknown, and no standard
guidelines exist for the detection and management of heterotopic ossification. Efforts
are ongoing to find a preventive solution at the genetic level. Research on functional
outcomes after surgical excision with or without prophylaxis are strongly encouraged.
Overall, risk factors for heterotopic ossification must be recognized to initiate
prophylaxis. If heterotopic ossification occurs postoperatively, surgeons should wait at
